questions.explanation: Borscht, a soup from Eastern Europe, gets its colour from beetroot pigments called betalains; cabbage is often added too.

questions.text: Which dairy product is made by churning cream?
questions.explanation: Churning damages the membranes around fat globules in cream so the fat clumps into butter, leaving buttermilk. Yogurt and kefir are fermented.

questions.text: Classic Indonesian satay sauce is based on which ground ingredient?
questions.explanation: Bumbu kacang for satay is made from fried, ground peanuts with chilli, garlic and kecap manis. Peanuts are legumes, not true nuts.

questions.text: Chocolate is made from the beans of which plant?
questions.explanation: Chocolate comes from fermented, roasted cacao beans. Carob is sometimes used as a chocolate substitute but comes from a different tree.

questions.text: Cheese fondue is a national dish of which country?
questions.explanation: Fondue, melted cheese with wine eaten by dipping bread, is Swiss; it was promoted as a national dish in the 1930s.

questions.text: Nori, used to wrap sushi rolls, is made from what?
questions.explanation: Nori is red algae (seaweed) shredded and dried into thin sheets, much like papermaking. Rice paper is used for spring rolls.

questions.text: Pad thai is a stir-fried noodle dish from which country?
questions.explanation: Pad thai is Thailand's stir-fried rice noodles with tamarind, fish sauce, egg and peanuts, popularised there in the mid-20th century.

questions.text: Which fruit is used in a classic French tarte Tatin?
questions.explanation: Tarte Tatin is an upside-down tart: apples are caramelised in butter and sugar under the pastry, then the tart is flipped.

questions.text: Which spice is the dried flower bud of a tree native to Indonesia's Maluku Islands?
questions.explanation: Cloves are unopened flower buds of a Maluku tree. Nutmeg also comes from Maluku, but it is the seed of a different tree.

questions.text: Mozzarella di bufala is made from which animal's milk?
questions.explanation: Mozzarella di bufala uses water buffalo milk, mainly from Campania in southern Italy; cow's-milk mozzarella is called fior di latte.

questions.text: Bulgur is made from which cereal grain?
questions.explanation: Bulgur is wheat that has been parboiled, dried and cracked; it is the main grain in the Levantine salad tabbouleh.

questions.text: What is the main ingredient of baba ghanoush?
questions.explanation: Baba ghanoush is a Levantine dip of roasted, mashed eggplant with tahini; the chickpea-based dip is hummus.

questions.text: Which pasta's name means 'little tongues' in Italian?
questions.explanation: Linguine comes from lingua, 'tongue', for its flat narrow shape. Orecchiette means 'little ears'.

questions.text: Which Japanese word names the savoury 'fifth basic taste'?
questions.explanation: Umami was identified in 1908 by chemist Kikunae Ikeda, who traced it to glutamate in kombu broth. Dashi is a stock, not a taste.

questions.text: Goulash, a paprika-rich stew, originated in which country?
questions.explanation: Goulash comes from Hungary, where gulyás means 'herdsman'; it later spread across the former Austro-Hungarian lands.

questions.text: Which mould gives Roquefort cheese its blue veins?
questions.explanation: Penicillium roqueforti makes the blue veins in Roquefort, a sheep's-milk cheese. Aspergillus oryzae is koji and Rhizopus makes tempeh.

questions.text: What is the French term for diced onion, carrot and celery used as a flavour base?
questions.explanation: Mirepoix is the classic onion-carrot-celery base for stocks and sauces. A roux is flour cooked in fat, used for thickening.

questions.text: What mainly gives Indonesian kecap manis its sweetness?
questions.explanation: Kecap manis is fermented soy sauce cooked down with palm sugar (gula aren or gula jawa), which makes it thick and syrupy.

questions.text: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Mercury orbits closest to the Sun, at an average of about 58 million km. Venus is second, yet it is the hotter planet.

questions.text: Who was the first human to travel into space?
questions.explanation: Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth once aboard Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961. The whole flight lasted about 108 minutes.

questions.text: Our solar system is located in which galaxy?
questions.explanation: The Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way. Andromeda, Sombrero and Whirlpool are separate galaxies far beyond it.

questions.text: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?
questions.explanation: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. Saturn is the second largest.

questions.text: Why can footprints remain on the Moon for a very long time?
questions.explanation: The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so no wind or rain erodes the prints. Only tiny micrometeorite impacts slowly wear them away.

questions.text: How many natural moons does Mars have?
questions.explanation: Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. They may be captured asteroids or debris from an ancient impact.

questions.text: An astronomical unit is based on the average distance between which two objects?
questions.explanation: One astronomical unit is about 150 million km, roughly the average Earth–Sun distance. It is now defined as an exact fixed length.

questions.text: A light-year measures what?
questions.explanation: Despite the word 'year', a light-year is a distance: how far light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion km.

questions.text: Which planet rotates on its side compared with most other planets?
questions.explanation: Uranus's axis is tilted about 98°, so it rolls around the Sun on its side. A giant ancient collision is the leading explanation.

questions.text: What is a supernova?
questions.explanation: A supernova is a star's powerful explosion, when a massive star's core collapses or a white dwarf ignites. It can briefly outshine a galaxy.

questions.text: Which planet has the Great Red Spot?
questions.explanation: The Great Red Spot is a giant, long-lived storm in Jupiter's atmosphere. It has been observed for well over a century.

questions.text: What was the name of the first artificial satellite?
questions.explanation: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957. Its radio beeps could be picked up by listeners around the world.

questions.text: Which planet is the hottest in our solar system?
questions.explanation: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping its surface around 465°C. Mercury is closer to the Sun but loses heat easily.

questions.text: What is the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can escape?
questions.explanation: At the event horizon, the escape speed equals the speed of light, so not even light can get out. It is a boundary, not a solid surface.

questions.text: Which space telescope launched in 2021 to study the early universe?
questions.explanation: Webb launched on 25 December 2021. It observes mainly in infrared, which lets it detect light from very distant early galaxies.

questions.text: What is the name of Saturn's largest moon?
questions.explanation: Titan is the only moon known to have a thick atmosphere. Europa and Io orbit Jupiter, while Phobos orbits Mars.

questions.text: Which planet has the shortest year?
questions.explanation: Mercury circles the Sun in about 88 Earth days because its orbit is the smallest and fastest. Venus takes about 225 days.

questions.text: What are comets mainly made of?
questions.explanation: Comets are 'dirty snowballs' of ice, dust and rock. Near the Sun, the ice turns to gas, forming a glowing coma and tails.

questions.text: Which star is closest to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away and belongs to the Alpha Centauri system. Sirius looks brightest at night but is farther away.

questions.text: What do astronomers call a planet orbiting a star outside our solar system?
questions.explanation: An exoplanet orbits a star other than the Sun. The first one around a Sun-like star was confirmed in 1995.

questions.text: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
questions.explanation: Armstrong stepped onto the Moon in July 1969 during Apollo 11. Aldrin followed him, while Collins stayed in lunar orbit.

questions.text: Which former ninth planet was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006?
questions.explanation: Pluto was reclassified because it has not cleared its orbit of other objects. Eris, a similar-sized body found in 2005, helped prompt the change.

questions.text: What element is the Sun mostly made of?
questions.explanation: About 73% of the Sun's mass is hydrogen. In its core, hydrogen fuses into helium, releasing the energy that makes the Sun shine.

questions.text: Which planet is often called Earth's twin because of its similar size?
questions.explanation: Venus is close to Earth in size and mass, but the 'twin' label is deceptive: its crushing CO₂ atmosphere makes it far hotter.

questions.text: What is a 'shooting star' really?
questions.explanation: It is a meteor: a small space rock burning up as it rushes through Earth's atmosphere. It is not a star at all.

questions.text: What is the name of the United States' civilian space agency?
questions.explanation: NASA was founded in 1958. ESA is Europe's space agency, JAXA is Japan's and ISRO is India's.

questions.text: Which planet is farthest from the Sun?
questions.explanation: Neptune orbits about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth does. Pluto can be farther, but it is a dwarf planet.

questions.text: What is a recognizable pattern of stars in the night sky called?
questions.explanation: Constellations like Orion are patterns seen from Earth; their stars are often at very different distances. Astronomers recognize 88.

questions.text: How long does Earth take to orbit the Sun once?
questions.explanation: One orbit takes about 365.25 days. That extra quarter day is why a leap day is added almost every four years.

questions.text: Which planet is third from the Sun?
questions.explanation: Earth comes third, after Mercury and Venus. Its distance lets liquid water exist on the surface, a key reason life thrives here.

questions.text: What causes the Moon's changing phases?
answers: Our changing view of its lit half
questions.explanation: The Sun always lights half the Moon; as it orbits Earth we see different amounts of that half. Earth's shadow only causes lunar eclipses.

questions.text: Gravity on the Moon is roughly what fraction of Earth's?
questions.explanation: Moon gravity is about 16.5% of Earth's, so a 60 kg person would weigh like a 10 kg object there. Their mass stays the same.

questions.text: The giant volcano Olympus Mons is found on which planet?
questions.explanation: Olympus Mons rises about 22 km, roughly two and a half times Everest's height. Low gravity and a crust that does not shift let it grow huge.

questions.text: What type of galaxy is the Milky Way?
questions.explanation: The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy with a central bar of stars. The Sun lies in a minor spiral arm about 26,000 light-years from the center.

questions.text: What is the region of icy bodies beyond Neptune's orbit called?
questions.explanation: The Kuiper Belt is home to Pluto and many other icy worlds. The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter, and Orion's Belt is three stars.

questions.text: Which moon of Jupiter is the largest moon in the solar system?
questions.explanation: Ganymede is even larger than the planet Mercury, and it is the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field.

questions.text: Who was the first woman to travel into space?
questions.explanation: Tereshkova flew aboard Vostok 6 in June 1963. Sally Ride became the first American woman in space twenty years later.

questions.text: Which planet takes longer to spin once on its axis than to orbit the Sun?
questions.explanation: Venus spins once every 243 Earth days but orbits the Sun in about 225. It also spins backward compared with most planets.

questions.text: Which spacecraft was the first to cross into interstellar space?
questions.explanation: Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause in 2012, leaving the bubble of solar wind around the Sun. Voyager 2 followed in 2018.

questions.text: Before becoming a white dwarf, what will the Sun swell into?
questions.explanation: In about 5 billion years the Sun will expand into a red giant. It lacks the mass to end as a neutron star or black hole.

questions.text: How many keys does a standard modern piano usually have?
questions.explanation: A standard modern piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black, spanning just over seven octaves from A0 to C8.

questions.text: In music, what does tempo describe?
questions.explanation: Tempo is the speed or pace of the beat, often given in beats per minute; volume is described by dynamics instead.

questions.text: Which is traditionally the highest female singing voice?
questions.explanation: Soprano is the highest standard female voice type; alto is the lowest, while tenor and baritone are male voices.

questions.text: A large group containing strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion is called what?
questions.explanation: An orchestra combines all four instrument families; a choir is singers, and a quartet has only four performers.

questions.text: Which clef is commonly used for higher-pitched notes?
questions.explanation: The treble (G) clef marks higher notes and is used for instruments like violin and flute; the bass (F) clef marks lower ones.

questions.text: The Beatles were formed in which English city?
questions.explanation: The Beatles formed in Liverpool in 1960 and built their early following at the city's Cavern Club.

questions.text: How many strings does a standard violin have?
questions.explanation: A violin has four strings tuned in fifths: G, D, A and E. Six strings is the standard guitar.

questions.text: What does crescendo instruct musicians to do?
questions.explanation: Crescendo, Italian for 'growing', means gradually louder; its opposite is decrescendo or diminuendo.

questions.text: Which family of instruments is mainly played by striking or shaking?
questions.explanation: Percussion instruments such as drums, cymbals and maracas sound when struck, shaken or scraped.

questions.text: Counting both ends, how many notes are there from C up to the next C?
questions.explanation: C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C: counting both ends of the scale gives eight notes, which is why the span is called an octave, from Latin for 'eighth'.

questions.text: Which instrument belongs to the brass family?
questions.explanation: The trumpet is brass: sound comes from the player's buzzing lips. Clarinet and oboe are woodwinds; violin is a string.

questions.text: How many lines are on a standard musical staff?
questions.explanation: A standard staff has five lines and four spaces; notes above or below it use short ledger lines.

questions.text: What does forte mean in musical notation?
questions.explanation: Forte (f) is Italian for 'strong' and means play loudly; piano (p) means softly.

questions.text: Which composer continued writing music after becoming largely deaf?
questions.explanation: Beethoven's hearing declined from his late 20s, yet he wrote major works like the Ninth Symphony when almost totally deaf.

questions.text: Which instrument uses a double reed?
questions.explanation: The oboe uses two blades of cane vibrating together. The saxophone uses a single reed, and the flute has no reed at all.

questions.text: What is a piece written for two performers called?
questions.explanation: A duet is for two performers; solo is one, trio is three and quartet is four.

questions.text: Reggae music originated in which country?
questions.explanation: Reggae developed in Jamaica in the late 1960s out of ska and rocksteady, and Bob Marley spread it worldwide.

questions.text: Which symbol raises a note by one semitone?
questions.explanation: A sharp (♯) raises a note by a semitone; a flat (♭) lowers it by one.

questions.text: A cappella music is performed primarily without what?
questions.explanation: A cappella, Italian for 'in the manner of the chapel', means singing without instrumental accompaniment.

questions.text: Which musical period came directly before the Classical period?
questions.explanation: The Baroque era (c. 1600–1750, Bach and Vivaldi) preceded the Classical era of Haydn and Mozart; Romantic came after.

questions.text: How many strings does a standard guitar have?
questions.explanation: A standard guitar has six strings, usually tuned E-A-D-G-B-E; the bass guitar typically has four.

questions.text: Which composer wrote The Four Seasons violin concertos?
questions.explanation: Antonio Vivaldi, a Venetian Baroque composer, published The Four Seasons around 1725 as four violin concertos.

questions.text: Which composer wrote the opera The Magic Flute?
questions.explanation: Mozart's The Magic Flute premiered in Vienna in 1791, just weeks before his death. Verdi and Puccini were later Italian opera composers.

questions.text: The didgeridoo is a traditional wind instrument from which country?
questions.explanation: The didgeridoo comes from Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia and is often made from a eucalyptus trunk hollowed by termites.

questions.text: In 4/4 time, how many beats does a whole note last?
questions.explanation: A whole note fills a whole 4/4 bar: four beats. A half note lasts two beats and a quarter note one.

questions.text: Which is the largest bowed string instrument in a standard orchestra?
questions.explanation: The double bass is the biggest and lowest-pitched bowed string in the orchestra; the cello is next in size.

questions.text: Gamelan is a traditional ensemble from which country?
questions.explanation: Gamelan comes from Java and Bali in Indonesia and is built mainly on bronze percussion such as gongs and metallophones.

questions.text: Which music genre originated in New Orleans in the early 20th century?
questions.explanation: Jazz grew from blues, ragtime and brass-band traditions in New Orleans around 1900. Samba arose in Brazil, polka in Central Europe.

questions.text: Flamenco music and dance are most associated with which country?
questions.explanation: Flamenco developed in Andalusia in southern Spain, blending Romani, Moorish and Andalusian influences. Tango is Argentina's dance.

questions.text: The sitar is closely tied to the classical music of which country?
questions.explanation: The sitar is a long-necked plucked lute central to Hindustani (North Indian) classical music, made famous abroad by Ravi Shankar.

questions.text: Which Italian term tells musicians to gradually slow down?
questions.explanation: Ritardando (rit.) means gradually slowing; accelerando is its opposite, speeding up. Fortissimo means very loud.

questions.text: Which composer wrote the music for the ballet Swan Lake?
questions.explanation: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake premiered at Moscow's Bolshoi Theatre in 1877; he also wrote The Nutcracker and Sleeping Beauty.

questions.text: What does a staccato marking tell a performer to do?
questions.explanation: Staccato, shown by a dot over or under a note, means short and separated; its opposite, legato, means smooth and connected.

questions.text: Which keyboard instrument sounds by plucking its strings?
questions.explanation: A harpsichord's keys lift jacks whose plectra (originally quills) pluck the strings. A clavichord strikes them with metal tangents.

questions.text: How many semitones are in one octave?
questions.explanation: An octave is divided into twelve semitones, which is why a piano repeats the same pattern of 12 white and black keys.

questions.text: What is a chord of three notes stacked in thirds called?
questions.explanation: A triad has a root, third and fifth, e.g. C-E-G. A cadence is a closing chord progression, not a single chord.

questions.text: How is the angklung, a bamboo instrument from West Java, played?
questions.explanation: Each angklung's bamboo tubes are tuned to one pitch and sound when shaken, so players work together to form melodies.

questions.text: Who composed the four-opera cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen?
questions.explanation: Richard Wagner's Ring cycle runs about 15 hours over four operas and premiered complete at Bayreuth in 1876.

questions.text: What is the interval from C up to the G above it called?
questions.explanation: Counting C, D, E, F, G gives five note names, so C to G is a fifth, spanning seven semitones. C to F would be a fourth.

questions.text: How many sharps are in the key signature of D major?
questions.explanation: D major has two sharps, F♯ and C♯. G major has one, and A major has three.

questions.text: What process lets plants turn sunlight into chemical energy?
questions.explanation: Plants use light energy to build glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. Respiration does the reverse, releasing stored energy.

questions.text: What is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth?
questions.explanation: The Amazon spans about 5.5 million km² across nine countries, mostly in Brazil. The Congo rainforest is the second largest.

questions.text: During evaporation, liquid water changes into what?
questions.explanation: Heat gives water molecules enough energy to escape as an invisible gas, water vapor. Clouds are tiny liquid droplets formed when vapor condenses.

questions.text: Igneous rock forms when which material cools and solidifies?
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks such as granite and basalt form from magma that cools underground or lava that cools at the surface.

questions.text: Most of Earth's protective ozone layer is found in which atmospheric layer?
questions.explanation: About 90% of atmospheric ozone lies in the stratosphere, roughly 15–35 km up, where it absorbs much of the Sun's harmful UV light.

questions.text: Corals are primarily made by colonies of what?
questions.explanation: Corals are animals: tiny polyps related to jellyfish that build limestone skeletons. Many host algae that supply them with food.

questions.text: Which scale is commonly used to rate tornado intensity?
questions.explanation: The Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale rates tornadoes from EF0 to EF5 based on damage. The Richter scale is for earthquakes; Beaufort is for wind.

questions.text: Mangrove forests are best adapted to which environment?
questions.explanation: Mangroves tolerate salty tidal water and use stilt roots and breathing roots to cope with waterlogged, low-oxygen mud.

questions.text: What is Earth's outermost solid layer called?
questions.explanation: The crust is Earth's thin rocky shell, about 5 km thick under the oceans and up to around 70 km under mountains.

questions.text: Auroras are mainly caused by charged particles interacting with what?
questions.explanation: Charged particles from the Sun, guided by Earth's magnetic field, hit gases high in the atmosphere and make them glow. Oxygen often gives green light.

questions.text: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of dry air and oxygen about 21%. Carbon dioxide is only a tiny fraction.

questions.text: What is the process by which rocks break down at Earth's surface?
questions.explanation: Weathering breaks rock down in place by physical, chemical or biological action. Erosion is the separate process that carries the pieces away.

questions.text: Which biome is characterized by permafrost?
questions.explanation: Tundra has permafrost, ground that stays frozen for at least two years in a row, which keeps trees and deep roots from growing.

questions.text: What is the largest layer of Earth by volume?
questions.explanation: The mantle makes up roughly 84% of Earth's volume. It is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly over long timescales.

questions.text: Which natural process moves water from plant leaves into the air?
questions.explanation: Plants release water vapor through tiny leaf pores called stomata. This transpiration helps pull water up from the roots.

questions.text: What type of cloud is most associated with thunderstorms?
questions.explanation: Cumulonimbus are towering storm clouds that can produce lightning, heavy rain and hail. Cirrus are thin, wispy clouds of ice high in the sky.

questions.text: Which instrument measures earthquakes?
questions.explanation: A seismograph records ground shaking from earthquakes. A barometer measures air pressure and an anemometer measures wind speed.

questions.text: Which ocean current helps warm western Europe?
questions.explanation: The Gulf Stream carries warm tropical water north across the Atlantic; its extension, the North Atlantic Current, helps keep western Europe milder.

questions.text: What is molten rock called after it reaches Earth's surface?
questions.explanation: Molten rock is called magma underground and lava once it erupts onto the surface. Basalt is a rock formed when lava cools.

questions.text: Which ecosystem stores large amounts of carbon in waterlogged soil?
questions.explanation: In waterlogged, low-oxygen soil, dead plants decay slowly and build up as peat. Peatlands cover only about 3% of land yet store vast amounts of carbon.

questions.text: What is the general name for rain, snow and hail?
questions.explanation: Precipitation is any water that falls from clouds to the ground. Condensation is the earlier step, when vapor turns into cloud droplets.

questions.text: Which type of rock forms from layers of sediment pressed together?
questions.explanation: Sandstone and limestone are sedimentary rocks, built from compacted layers of sand, mud or shells. These layers often preserve fossils.

questions.text: What is a hot spring that periodically shoots water and steam into the air?
questions.explanation: Geysers erupt when underground water heated by hot rock boils and bursts out, as at Old Faithful in Yellowstone. Volcanoes erupt molten rock.

questions.text: What do we call the natural home where a plant or animal lives?
questions.explanation: A habitat provides the food, water, shelter and conditions an organism needs. A population is a group of one species living in an area.

questions.text: What are the preserved remains or traces of ancient life in rock called?
questions.explanation: Fossils include bones, shells, imprints and even footprints. They usually form when remains are buried quickly in sediment.

questions.text: Which biome typically gets less than 250 mm of rain a year?
questions.explanation: Deserts are defined by low rainfall, not by heat, so cold places such as much of Antarctica count as deserts too.

questions.text: What mainly causes ocean tides?
questions.explanation: The Moon's pull makes ocean water bulge on the sides of Earth facing toward and away from it. The Sun's gravity adds a smaller effect.

questions.text: What is a series of huge sea waves usually caused by an undersea earthquake?
questions.explanation: A tsunami forms when the seafloor suddenly shifts and displaces water. In deep ocean it moves fast but low, then grows tall near the coast.

questions.text: What is a large, slowly moving mass of ice on land called?
questions.explanation: Glaciers form where snow builds up and compresses into ice that flows under its own weight. Icebergs are chunks that break off into water.

questions.text: What green pigment in plants captures light for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green, which is why leaves look green. Carotene gives carrots their orange color.

questions.text: What seasonal wind shift brings heavy summer rains to South Asia?
questions.explanation: Monsoon winds reverse with the seasons; in summer, moist air blows from the ocean onto warmer land. Indonesia's rainy season is monsoon-driven too.

questions.text: Marble is which type of rock?
questions.explanation: Marble forms when limestone is transformed by heat and pressure deep underground, and that kind of change defines metamorphic rock.

questions.text: Earth's outer shell is broken into large moving pieces called what?
questions.explanation: Tectonic plates drift a few centimeters a year over the hotter mantle below. Earthquakes and volcanoes cluster along their edges.

questions.text: What is a deep, steep-sided valley carved by a river called?
questions.explanation: Canyons form as rivers cut down through rock over millions of years. Arizona's Grand Canyon was carved largely by the Colorado River.

questions.text: What landform builds up where a river drops sediment at its mouth?
questions.explanation: A river slows as it meets the sea or a lake and drops its sediment, building a delta. The name comes from the Greek letter Δ, after the Nile's.

questions.text: What are organisms like fungi and many bacteria that break down dead matter called?
questions.explanation: Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead plants and animals back into the soil. Producers, such as plants, make their own food.

questions.text: Hurricanes and typhoons are regional names for what kind of storm?
questions.explanation: They are the same phenomenon: called a hurricane in the Atlantic and a typhoon in the northwest Pacific. Tornadoes are far smaller.

questions.text: Which mineral is rated 10, the top of the Mohs hardness scale?
questions.explanation: Diamond defines 10 on the Mohs scale. Corundum, the mineral of rubies and sapphires, is 9, though diamond is several times harder.

questions.text: Which supercontinent joined nearly all of Earth's land about 250 million years ago?
questions.explanation: Pangaea later split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south. Rodinia was a much older supercontinent, about a billion years ago.

questions.text: Roughly what share of energy passes from one level of a food chain to the next?
questions.explanation: By the '10% rule', most energy is lost as heat through life processes at each level. That is why food chains rarely exceed four or five levels.

questions.text: Thor is a god from which mythology?
questions.explanation: Thor is the Norse god of thunder and a protector of humankind. The English word Thursday comes from 'Thor's day'.

questions.text: Who is the king of the gods in Greek mythology?
questions.explanation: Zeus ruled the gods from Mount Olympus and wielded the thunderbolt. His brother Hades, by contrast, ruled the underworld.

questions.text: Anansi, the famous trickster, often appears as which creature?
questions.explanation: Anansi is a spider trickster from the Akan folklore of Ghana; his tales spread to the Caribbean through the Atlantic slave trade.

questions.text: Which legendary bird is said to rise again from its ashes?
questions.explanation: The phoenix bursts into flame at the end of its long life and is reborn from the ashes, making it a symbol of renewal.

questions.text: Which creature was said to live inside the Labyrinth of Crete?
questions.explanation: King Minos kept the Minotaur, half man and half bull, in the Labyrinth that Daedalus built for him on Crete.

questions.text: Ra was associated with the Sun in which ancient mythology?
questions.explanation: Ra, the Egyptian sun god, was believed to sail across the sky by day and through the underworld by night. He was often merged with Amun as Amun-Ra.

questions.text: In Norse mythology, what is the name of Odin's spear?
questions.explanation: Gungnir, forged by dwarves, was said never to miss its target. Mjolnir is Thor's hammer, Gram is Sigurd's sword and Gáe Bulg is the spear of the Irish hero Cú Chulainn.

questions.text: According to Greek myth, looking directly at Medusa could turn a person into what?
questions.explanation: Medusa, a Gorgon with snakes for hair, turned onlookers to stone. Perseus beheaded her by watching her reflection in a polished shield.

questions.text: In many Chinese traditions, dragons are strongly associated with what?
questions.explanation: Unlike the fearsome dragons of Western tales, Chinese dragons are benevolent, linked to rain, water, imperial power and luck.

questions.text: What is the name of King Arthur's legendary sword?
questions.explanation: Excalibur is often said to be a gift from the Lady of the Lake. Durandal belonged to Roland, Kusanagi is from Japanese myth, and Gram was Sigurd's.

questions.text: Who ruled the underworld in Greek mythology?
questions.explanation: Hades ruled the realm of the dead with his queen Persephone, whom he had carried off from the world above.

questions.text: Odin is a major god in which mythology?
questions.explanation: Odin, chief of the Norse gods, gave up an eye in exchange for wisdom. English 'Wednesday' comes from Woden, the Old English form of his name.

questions.text: Which Greek hero defeated the Minotaur?
questions.explanation: Theseus slew the Minotaur and found his way out of the Labyrinth using a ball of thread given to him by Ariadne.

questions.text: The goddess Amaterasu is associated with which tradition?
questions.explanation: Amaterasu is the Shinto sun goddess, and Japan's imperial family traditionally claims descent from her. Her shrine at Ise is Shinto's holiest.

questions.text: What kind of creature is a centaur?
questions.explanation: Centaurs have a human upper body on a horse's body. The wise centaur Chiron tutored heroes such as Achilles and Jason.

questions.text: Which Greek hero was famous for completing twelve labors?
questions.explanation: Heracles (Hercules to the Romans) performed twelve labours as penance, including slaying the Nemean lion and cleaning the Augean stables.

questions.text: Quetzalcoatl was a feathered serpent deity of which culture?
questions.explanation: Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent, was linked to wind and learning. The Aztecs inherited him from older Mesoamerican cultures; the Maya called him Kukulkan.

questions.text: In Norse mythology, what is Yggdrasil?
questions.explanation: Yggdrasil is a giant ash tree whose branches and roots connect the nine worlds of Norse cosmology.

questions.text: Which creature guards the entrance to the Greek underworld?
questions.explanation: Cerberus, the three-headed hound of Hades, let the dead enter the underworld but stopped them from leaving.

questions.text: In Arthurian legend, who is the wizard and adviser to Arthur?
questions.explanation: Merlin guided Arthur from birth and, in many tellings, arranged the sword-in-the-stone test. Mordred was the traitor who fought Arthur at Camlann.

questions.text: Which Greek god ruled the sea?
questions.explanation: Poseidon carried a trident and could stir up storms and earthquakes. The Romans identified him with Neptune.

questions.text: What is the name of the winged horse in Greek mythology?
questions.explanation: Pegasus sprang from Medusa's neck when Perseus beheaded her and later carried the hero Bellerophon. Bucephalus was Alexander the Great's real horse.

questions.text: Who is the Greek goddess of wisdom and military strategy?
questions.explanation: Athena was born fully armed from the head of Zeus. The city of Athens took her name, and the owl became her symbol.

questions.text: Which Greek hero's only weak spot was his heel?
questions.explanation: His mother Thetis dipped him in the River Styx, holding him by the heel. Paris killed him with an arrow there, hence the phrase 'Achilles heel'.

questions.text: In Norse mythology, what is the home of the gods called?
questions.explanation: Asgard, home of the Aesir gods, was linked to Midgard, the world of humans, by the rainbow bridge Bifrost.

questions.text: What is the Roman name for Zeus?
questions.explanation: Jupiter was king of the Roman gods, matching Zeus. Mars matches Ares, Neptune matches Poseidon and Mercury matches Hermes.

questions.text: In Greek myth, who opened a jar that released evils into the world?
questions.explanation: Pandora, the first woman, opened a jar (later retold as a box) given by the gods; only Hope remained inside.

questions.text: Which Egyptian god is usually shown with the head of a jackal?
questions.explanation: Anubis guarded tombs and oversaw embalming. Horus, by contrast, has a falcon's head and Thoth an ibis's head.

questions.text: Which legendary outlaw of Sherwood Forest robbed the rich to give to the poor?
questions.explanation: Robin Hood and his Merry Men defied the Sheriff of Nottingham in English ballads. William Tell is a Swiss hero famed for his archery.

questions.text: In Greek myth, who flew too close to the Sun on wings of wax and feathers?
questions.explanation: Daedalus built the wings so he and his son Icarus could escape Crete. Icarus ignored his warning, the wax melted and he fell into the sea.

questions.text: Which Hindu god has the head of an elephant?
questions.explanation: Ganesha, son of Shiva and Parvati, is revered as the remover of obstacles and the patron of arts and learning.

questions.text: In Norse mythology, what is the name of Odin's eight-legged horse?
questions.explanation: Sleipnir could gallop over land, sea and air. Fenrir is a giant wolf, Huginn one of Odin's two ravens and Ratatoskr a squirrel.

questions.text: Which Trojan hero fled Troy and, in Roman legend, became an ancestor of the Romans?
questions.explanation: Virgil's Aeneid follows Aeneas from burning Troy to Italy, where his descendants Romulus and Remus would later found Rome.

questions.text: Which ancient epic follows a king of Uruk on a quest for immortality?
questions.explanation: From ancient Mesopotamia, Gilgamesh is among the oldest surviving works of literature; its best-known version was written on clay tablets.

questions.text: Which Norse trickster god is the father of the giant wolf Fenrir?
questions.explanation: Loki fathered Fenrir with the giantess Angrboda. Tyr, a tempting pick, lost his hand when the gods bound the wolf.

questions.text: In the Ramayana, Sita is the wife of which hero?
questions.explanation: Rama, an avatar of Vishnu, rescues Sita from the demon king Ravana with Hanuman's help. Arjuna, Krishna and Bhima belong to the Mahabharata.

questions.text: In Greek myth, who ferries the souls of the dead across the underworld river?
questions.explanation: Charon demanded a coin, so Greeks buried their dead with an obol. Hermes guided souls to the riverbank but did not row them across.

questions.text: In Egyptian myth, what was weighed against the feather of Ma'at to judge the dead?
questions.explanation: Egyptians saw the heart as the seat of thought and conscience. A heart heavier than the feather was devoured by the monster Ammit.

questions.text: In Norse mythology, what is the foretold final battle and doom of the gods called?
questions.explanation: At Ragnarok, Odin is swallowed by Fenrir and Thor dies fighting the World Serpent. Valhalla, by contrast, is Odin's hall of slain warriors.

questions.text: Which Japanese storm god slew the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi?
questions.explanation: Susanoo, Amaterasu's brother, got the serpent drunk on sake before killing it, then found the sword Kusanagi inside its tail.

questions.text: In traditional painting, which set is commonly taught as the primary colors?
questions.explanation: The traditional RYB model treats red, yellow and blue as the primaries for mixing paint. Red, green and blue are the primaries of light (RGB).

questions.text: Which technique helps artists create the illusion of depth on a flat surface?
questions.explanation: Perspective makes distant objects look smaller and lines converge. Brunelleschi formalized linear perspective in early 15th-century Florence.

questions.text: A sculpture is normally considered what kind of artwork?
questions.explanation: A sculpture has height, width and depth, so it can be viewed from many angles, unlike a flat painting or drawing.

questions.text: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.explanation: Leonardo began the Mona Lisa around 1503; it hangs in the Louvre in Paris. Michelangelo and Raphael were fellow giants of the High Renaissance.

questions.text: On a traditional color wheel, which color is complementary to red?
questions.explanation: Complementary colors sit opposite each other on the wheel. Green mixes the other two primaries, yellow and blue, so it is red's opposite.

questions.text: The Bauhaus school was founded in which country?
questions.explanation: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919. It later moved to Dessau and Berlin before closing under Nazi pressure in 1933.

questions.text: Typography is the art of arranging what?
questions.explanation: Typography covers choosing typefaces, sizes, spacing and layout so that text is easy to read and pleasing to look at.

questions.text: A traditional fresco is painted onto what?
questions.explanation: In true (buon) fresco, pigments are applied to wet lime plaster and bind as it dries, becoming part of the wall itself.

questions.text: In perspective drawing, parallel lines may appear to meet at what?
questions.explanation: Parallel lines receding from the viewer appear to converge at a vanishing point, usually on the horizon line.

questions.text: Origami is most closely associated with which country?
questions.explanation: Origami, from Japanese 'oru' (fold) and 'kami' (paper), is the art of folding paper into shapes, usually without cutting or glue.

questions.text: Which artist painted The Starry Night?
questions.explanation: Van Gogh painted The Starry Night in 1889 from his room at the asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence; it is now in MoMA, New York.

questions.text: What does negative space refer to in design?
questions.explanation: Negative space is the empty area around and between subjects. Designers use it cleverly, as in the hidden arrow of the FedEx logo.

questions.text: Which art movement is closely associated with Claude Monet?
questions.explanation: Monet's Impression, Sunrise (1872) gave Impressionism its name; the movement captured fleeting light with loose, visible brushstrokes.

questions.text: What is a monochromatic color scheme based on?
questions.explanation: A monochromatic scheme uses one hue in lighter tints and darker shades. Two opposite hues would form a complementary scheme instead.

questions.text: Which material is traditionally fired in a kiln?
questions.explanation: Firing clay at high heat in a kiln hardens it permanently into ceramic, such as earthenware, stoneware or porcelain.

questions.text: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
questions.explanation: Michelangelo painted the ceiling in 1508–1512 for Pope Julius II, including The Creation of Adam, though he saw himself mainly as a sculptor.

questions.text: In digital design, what does RGB stand for?
questions.explanation: Screens mix red, green and blue light additively; all three at full strength make white. Printing uses CMYK inks instead.

questions.text: Which style uses small dots of color that blend visually?
questions.explanation: Georges Seurat and Paul Signac developed Pointillism in the 1880s; the viewer's eye blends the dots, as in Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte.

questions.text: What is kerning in typography?
questions.explanation: Kerning adjusts the space between specific letter pairs, such as 'AV', so they look even. Tracking changes spacing across a whole word or line.

questions.text: Which architect designed Barcelona's Park Güell?
questions.explanation: Gaudí designed Park Güell (1900–1914) for patron Eusebi Güell, with mosaic-clad terraces and a famous tiled lizard. The other two Catalans were fellow Modernisme architects.

questions.text: Who painted The Persistence of Memory, with its melting clocks?
questions.explanation: Dalí painted the soft, melting watches in 1931 against a dreamlike Catalan coast. Magritte is known instead for his bowler-hatted men.

questions.text: Which Dutch artist painted Girl with a Pearl Earring?
questions.explanation: Vermeer painted it around 1665 in Delft; it belongs to the Mauritshuis in The Hague. Rubens, a tempting pick, was Flemish, not Dutch.

questions.text: Which Spanish artist co-founded Cubism with Georges Braque?
questions.explanation: Picasso and Braque developed Cubism around 1907–1914, showing subjects from several viewpoints at once as broken, geometric forms.

questions.text: What color do you get by mixing red and white paint?
questions.explanation: Adding white to a color makes a tint, a lighter version of it, so pink is a tint of red. Red with yellow would make orange instead.

questions.text: Michelangelo's marble statue David is displayed in which Italian city?
questions.explanation: Carved in 1501–1504, David stood outside Florence's Palazzo Vecchio until 1873, when it moved indoors to the Galleria dell'Accademia.

questions.text: Who painted The Scream?
questions.explanation: Norwegian artist Edvard Munch made several versions of The Scream from 1893, an icon of Expressionism. Klimt was an Austrian known for gilded works.

questions.text: On what do painters traditionally mix their paints?
questions.explanation: A palette is a flat board, often with a thumb hole, for mixing colors. An easel, by contrast, is the stand that holds the canvas.

questions.text: Andy Warhol is a leading figure of which art movement?
questions.explanation: With works like Campbell's Soup Cans and his Marilyn prints, Warhol turned mass-produced everyday imagery into art, the core idea of Pop Art.

questions.text: Which Mexican painter is famous for her vivid self-portraits?
questions.explanation: About a third of Frida Kahlo's paintings are self-portraits, often drawing on Mexican folk art and her long struggle with injury.

questions.text: In batik, what substance is applied to cloth to resist the dye?
questions.explanation: Artisans draw hot wax onto cloth with a canting or stamp it with a copper cap; waxed areas resist the dye. UNESCO recognized Indonesian batik in 2009.

questions.text: Which Italian artist painted The Birth of Venus?
questions.explanation: Botticelli painted it in the 1480s in Florence. It shows Venus arriving on a shell and hangs in the city's Uffizi Gallery.

questions.text: Which Dutch master painted The Night Watch?
questions.explanation: Rembrandt finished The Night Watch in 1642. This group portrait of Amsterdam civic guards, famed for its dramatic light, hangs in the Rijksmuseum.

questions.text: Which architectural style is known for pointed arches and flying buttresses?
questions.explanation: Gothic builders used pointed arches and flying buttresses to raise tall walls filled with stained glass. Romanesque churches used round arches.

questions.text: Which art movement, led by André Breton, explored dreams and the unconscious?
questions.explanation: Breton's 1924 Surrealist Manifesto, inspired by Freud, urged artists to tap the unconscious mind; Dalí and Magritte became leading Surrealists.

questions.text: In CMYK printing, what does the K stand for?
questions.explanation: K is the 'key' plate, which prints the black detail the other colors are aligned to. C, M and Y stand for cyan, magenta and yellow.

questions.text: Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa is what kind of artwork?
questions.explanation: Part of the ukiyo-e series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (c. 1831), it was printed from carved wooden blocks, one for each color.

questions.text: What does chiaroscuro mean in painting?
answers: Strong contrast of light and dark
questions.explanation: Italian for 'light-dark', chiaroscuro uses bold contrasts to model solid form and drama, as Caravaggio did. Painting on wet plaster is fresco.

questions.text: Which Renaissance painter created the fresco The School of Athens?
questions.explanation: Raphael painted it in 1509–1511 in the Vatican's Stanza della Segnatura. Perugino, a tempting pick, was Raphael's teacher.

questions.text: Piet Mondrian's grids of primary colors belong to which Dutch movement?
questions.explanation: De Stijl ('The Style'), founded in 1917 with Theo van Doesburg, reduced art to straight lines, primary colors, black and white.

questions.text: Who painted The Arrest of Prince Diponegoro (1857)?
questions.explanation: Raden Saleh, a pioneer of modern Indonesian painting, answered Dutch painter Nicolaas Pieneman's version of the scene with a more dignified Diponegoro.

questions.text: In which city can you find the Eiffel Tower?
questions.explanation: The Eiffel Tower is the iron lattice tower in Paris. Rome's famous ancient arena is the Colosseum.

questions.text: The Colosseum is a famous landmark in which city?
questions.explanation: The Colosseum is an ancient Roman amphitheater. Its name and role connect it to Rome, rather than the Greek monuments of Athens.

questions.text: The Taj Mahal is located in which Indian city?
questions.explanation: The Taj Mahal is in Agra, not India's capital New Delhi. Keep the monument's city separate from the country's capital.

questions.text: Machu Picchu was built high in the mountains of which country?
questions.explanation: Machu Picchu is an Inca site in the Peruvian Andes. The mountain range spans several countries, so Andes alone is not enough to identify Peru.

questions.text: The ancient rock-cut city of Petra is located in which country?
questions.explanation: Petra is known for buildings carved into rose-colored rock in Jordan. It is a rock-cut city, not one of Egypt's pyramid complexes.

questions.text: Christ the Redeemer overlooks which Brazilian city?
questions.explanation: Christ the Redeemer overlooks Rio de Janeiro. Brasilia is the national capital, but not the home of this statue.

questions.text: Which landmark stretches for thousands of kilometers across northern China?
questions.explanation: The clue describes a defensive wall. The Grand Canal is a waterway and the Silk Road is a network of trade routes.

questions.text: Big Ben, the great bell in the Elizabeth Tower, is part of which London building?
questions.explanation: Big Ben is the nickname of the Great Bell in the Elizabeth Tower, the clock tower at the north end of the Palace of Westminster, where Parliament meets.

questions.text: The famous Leaning Tower is found in which Italian city?
questions.explanation: The leaning bell tower belongs to Pisa's cathedral complex. Its tilt is the distinguishing feature in this question.

questions.text: The Statue of Liberty stands on an island in which city?
questions.explanation: The Statue of Liberty stands in New York Harbor. Washington, D.C. is the capital, but is not the statue's location.

questions.text: Antoni Gaudí designed which basilica in Barcelona?
questions.explanation: Sagrada Familia is Gaudí's basilica in Barcelona. The Sistine Chapel and St Mark's Basilica are in Italy, and Sacré-Coeur is in Paris.

questions.text: Angkor Wat appears on the national flag of which country?
questions.explanation: Cambodia's flag displays Angkor Wat in its center. The temple silhouette is the identifying clue.

questions.text: The Burj Khalifa skyscraper, opened in 2010, is in which city?
questions.explanation: Burj Khalifa is in Dubai. Abu Dhabi is another city in the United Arab Emirates, so the country alone does not distinguish them.

questions.text: The Golden Gate Bridge connects San Francisco with which county?
questions.explanation: The bridge crosses the Golden Gate strait from San Francisco to Marin County on the north side.

questions.text: Which Australian city is home to the sail-shaped Opera House?
questions.explanation: The Opera House's shell-like roof beside the harbor is a visual landmark of Sydney, not Melbourne.

questions.text: The giant Moai statues were carved on which remote island?
questions.explanation: The Moai are associated with Easter Island, also called Rapa Nui. They are carved figures, not buildings.

questions.text: Mount Rushmore is located in which U.S. state?
questions.explanation: Mount Rushmore is in South Dakota. The mountain setting can make the nearby western states tempting distractors.

questions.text: Neuschwanstein Castle is located in which country?
questions.explanation: Neuschwanstein is in Bavaria, a region of Germany. Its Alpine setting does not make it an Austrian or Swiss castle.

questions.text: Chichen Itza was built by which ancient civilization?
questions.explanation: Chichen Itza is a Maya site in Mexico. Machu Picchu, by contrast, is associated with the Inca.

questions.text: Hagia Sophia is a historic landmark in which city?
questions.explanation: Hagia Sophia is in Istanbul, historically known as Constantinople. The two city names refer to the same place in different eras.

questions.text: The Parthenon, an ancient Greek temple from the 5th century BC, stands in which city?
questions.explanation: The Parthenon crowns the Acropolis of Athens and was built for the goddess Athena, the city's patron. Rome has the similarly named Pantheon.

questions.text: Stonehenge, the prehistoric stone circle, is in which English county?
questions.explanation: Stonehenge stands on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, southern England. It was built in stages, beginning around 3000 BC.

questions.text: Red Square and the colorful domes of St Basil's Cathedral are in which city?
questions.explanation: Red Square lies beside the Kremlin in Moscow. Saint Petersburg was once Russia's imperial capital, but these landmarks are in Moscow.

questions.text: The glass pyramid designed by I. M. Pei is the main entrance to which Paris museum?
questions.explanation: I. M. Pei's glass pyramid, opened in 1989, leads into the Louvre. The Musée d'Orsay, across the Seine, occupies a former railway station.

questions.text: The 9th-century Buddhist temple Borobudur is on which Indonesian island?
questions.explanation: Borobudur stands in Magelang, Central Java. Built under the Sailendra dynasty, its terraces are lined with hundreds of Buddha statues and relief panels.

questions.text: Prambanan, the 9th-century temple compound near Yogyakarta, was built for which religion?
questions.explanation: Prambanan is a Hindu compound whose main temples honor the Trimurti: Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma. Nearby Borobudur, by contrast, is Buddhist.

questions.text: The Forbidden City, palace of the Chinese emperors, is in which city?
questions.explanation: The Forbidden City in Beijing housed Ming and Qing emperors for nearly 500 years. Today it is the Palace Museum.

questions.text: The Brandenburg Gate, topped by a chariot sculpture, is in which city?
questions.explanation: The Brandenburg Gate stands in Berlin. Once next to the Berlin Wall, it became a symbol of German reunification after 1989.

questions.text: Fushimi Inari Taisha, a shrine with thousands of red torii gates, is in which Japanese city?
questions.explanation: Fushimi Inari Taisha is in southern Kyoto. Its vermilion torii, donated by people and businesses, line trails up Mount Inari.

questions.text: The Alhambra, a palace and fortress built by Moorish rulers, is in which Spanish city?
questions.explanation: The Alhambra overlooks Granada and was mainly built by the Nasrid dynasty. Córdoba is known for a different Moorish landmark, its Great Mosque.

questions.text: Visitors toss coins into the Trevi Fountain in which city?
questions.explanation: The Baroque Trevi Fountain, completed in 1762, is in Rome. Tradition says a coin thrown over your shoulder means you will return to the city.

questions.text: Which London bridge has two Gothic-style towers and a roadway that lifts to let ships pass?
questions.explanation: Tower Bridge, opened in 1894, is a bascule bridge whose roadway rises for river traffic. It is often mistaken for the much plainer London Bridge.

questions.text: The Space Needle, built for the 1962 World's Fair, is in which city?
questions.explanation: The Space Needle was built in Seattle for the 1962 Century 21 Exposition. Toronto's famous tower is the CN Tower.

questions.text: The Petronas Twin Towers, linked by a skybridge, are in which city?
questions.explanation: The Petronas Twin Towers in Kuala Lumpur were completed in 1998. A two-level skybridge joins the towers at the 41st and 42nd floors.

questions.text: The plains of Bagan, dotted with thousands of ancient Buddhist temples, are in which country?
questions.explanation: Most of Bagan's temples were built in the 11th to 13th centuries, when it was the capital of the Pagan Kingdom in today's Myanmar.

questions.text: Cappadocia, famous for 'fairy chimney' rock formations and hot-air balloons, is in which country?
questions.explanation: Cappadocia is in central Turkey. Its fairy chimneys were eroded from soft volcanic tuff, which people also carved into homes and churches.

questions.text: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, carved down into solid rock, are in which country?
questions.explanation: Lalibela in northern Ethiopia has 11 medieval churches cut from rock and named after King Lalibela. Many were carved downward into the ground.

questions.text: Charles Bridge, a statue-lined medieval stone bridge, crosses the river in which city?
questions.explanation: Charles Bridge crosses the Vltava in Prague; work began in 1357 under Charles IV. Budapest's famous Chain Bridge spans the Danube instead.

questions.text: The Potala Palace, former residence of the Dalai Lama, rises above which city?
questions.explanation: The Potala Palace in Lhasa, Tibet, was the Dalai Lamas' winter residence until 1959. Thimphu, the capital of Bhutan, is a different Himalayan city.

questions.text: The Great Mosque of Djenné, built of sun-dried mud brick, is in which country?
questions.explanation: The Great Mosque of Djenné is in Mali; the present building dates from 1907. Its mud walls are replastered by the community in an annual festival.

questions.text: Which school does Harry Potter attend?
questions.explanation: Hogwarts is Harry's school of witchcraft and wizardry; Nevermore belongs to Wednesday's story.

questions.text: In Friends, what is the group's regular coffee shop called?
questions.explanation: Central Perk is the coffee shop where the Friends group regularly gathers, not their apartment.

questions.text: Which fictional town is central to Stranger Things?
questions.explanation: Hawkins is the fictional town at the center of Stranger Things; Riverdale belongs to a different series.

questions.text: What is Wednesday Addams's school in the Netflix series?
questions.explanation: Wednesday attends Nevermore Academy, a school for outcasts in the Netflix series.

questions.text: Who captains the Straw Hat Pirates in One Piece?
questions.explanation: Luffy is the captain. Zoro and Sanji are members of his crew, while Shanks leads a different crew.

questions.text: Which color pill does Neo take to learn the truth in The Matrix?
questions.explanation: Neo chooses the red pill to discover reality. The blue pill represents returning to his familiar life.

questions.text: What was Darth Vader's name before he became a Sith?
questions.explanation: Anakin Skywalker becomes Darth Vader. Luke is his son, not his former identity.

questions.text: What species is Chewbacca?
questions.explanation: Chewbacca is a Wookiee. Ewoks are the smaller furry beings associated with Endor.

questions.text: Which ship is famously flown by Han Solo and Chewbacca?
questions.explanation: The Millennium Falcon is Han and Chewbacca's ship. Enterprise belongs to Star Trek.

questions.text: In The Lord of the Rings, where must the One Ring be destroyed?
questions.explanation: The Ring must return to the fire of Mount Doom, where it was forged; Rivendell is a refuge, not its destination.

questions.text: What is the surname of the family in The Simpsons?
questions.explanation: The family surname is Simpson; the show's plural title refers to the whole family.

questions.text: Which city is the main setting of the TV show Friends?
questions.explanation: Friends follows the group in New York City, with their apartments and Central Perk as recurring settings.

questions.text: Which actor plays Barbie in the 2023 live-action film?
questions.explanation: Margot Robbie plays Barbie in the 2023 film. The question asks for the performer, not the director.

questions.text: Who directed the 2023 film Barbie?
questions.explanation: Greta Gerwig directed Barbie (2023); Margot Robbie is its lead performer.

questions.text: In Jurassic Park (1993), what kind of creatures are brought back to life?
questions.explanation: Jurassic Park's theme park contains recreated dinosaurs, not mythical dragons.

questions.text: What is the name of the archaeologist played by Harrison Ford in Raiders of the Lost Ark?
questions.explanation: Harrison Ford plays the archaeologist Indiana Jones. Han Solo is another of his roles, in Star Wars.

questions.text: Which sitcom follows employees of Dunder Mifflin's Scranton branch?
questions.explanation: The Office's US version follows Dunder Mifflin's Scranton employees. The other options follow different workplaces.

questions.text: Which TV series features the fictional continent Westeros?
questions.explanation: Westeros is a fictional continent in Game of Thrones, not a real country.

questions.text: What is the name of the blue-skinned species in Avatar (2009)?
questions.explanation: The Na'vi are the blue-skinned people of Pandora in Avatar; the other names come from different fictional universes.

questions.text: In the original Karate Kid film, who teaches Daniel karate?
questions.explanation: In the 1984 film, Mr. Miyagi mentors Daniel. Mr. Han mentors a different protagonist in the 2010 film.

questions.text: In Breaking Bad, what subject does Walter White teach before turning to crime?
questions.explanation: Walter is a high-school chemistry teacher who uses his expertise to make methamphetamine after a cancer diagnosis.

questions.text: Which fictional detective lives at 221B Baker Street in London?
questions.explanation: Arthur Conan Doyle's Holmes shares 221B Baker Street with Dr Watson; Poirot and Miss Marple are Agatha Christie's detectives.

questions.text: Squid Game, the hit 2021 Netflix survival drama, comes from which country?
questions.explanation: Squid Game was created by South Korean director Hwang Dong-hyuk, and its deadly contests are based on Korean children's games.

questions.text: What is the name of Harry Potter's snowy owl?
questions.explanation: Hedwig is Harry's snowy owl; Errol belongs to the Weasley family, and Fawkes is Dumbledore's phoenix.

questions.text: In The Hunger Games, which district is Katniss Everdeen from?
questions.explanation: Katniss comes from District 12, a poor coal-mining district, and volunteers to take her younger sister's place in the Games.

questions.text: Which Star Trek character is half human and half Vulcan?
questions.explanation: Spock has a Vulcan father and a human mother, so he balances logic and emotion; Data is an android and Worf is a Klingon.

questions.text: In Doctor Who, what does the TARDIS look like from the outside?
questions.explanation: The TARDIS's faulty chameleon circuit leaves it stuck looking like a blue British police box, and it is famously bigger on the inside.

questions.text: Who wrote the 1937 novel The Hobbit?
questions.explanation: Tolkien wrote The Hobbit before The Lord of the Rings; his friend C.S. Lewis wrote the Narnia books.

questions.text: In Game of Thrones, which castle is the ancestral seat of House Stark?
questions.explanation: Winterfell is the Starks' home in the North; Casterly Rock is the seat of House Lannister.

questions.text: Which 1982 Ridley Scott film follows Rick Deckard, a hunter of rogue replicants?
questions.explanation: Blade Runner, loosely based on a Philip K. Dick novel, stars Harrison Ford as Deckard; Scott's Alien came earlier, in 1979.

questions.text: In the 1939 film The Wizard of Oz, what color are Dorothy's magic slippers?
questions.explanation: The film made the slippers ruby red to show off Technicolor; in L. Frank Baum's original novel they are silver shoes.

questions.text: In Pirates of the Caribbean, what is the name of Captain Jack Sparrow's ship?
questions.explanation: Jack's ship is the Black Pearl, with its black sails; the Flying Dutchman is the ghostly ship captained by Davy Jones.

questions.text: Which fictional British secret agent has the code number 007?
questions.explanation: Ian Fleming's James Bond is agent 007 of MI6, where the 00 prefix means a licence to kill; Jason Bourne is an American agent.

questions.text: Which board game features properties such as Boardwalk and Park Place?
questions.explanation: Boardwalk and Park Place are the priciest properties in the US edition of Monopoly; the UK edition calls them Mayfair and Park Lane.

questions.text: In Back to the Future, what speed must the DeLorean reach to travel through time?
questions.explanation: Doc Brown's DeLorean time machine jumps through time at 88 miles per hour, powered by its flux capacitor.

questions.text: Which TV drama follows the aristocratic Crawley family and their servants?
questions.explanation: Downton Abbey is set at the Crawleys' English country estate in the early 1900s; The Crown is about the real British royal family.

questions.text: Which Netflix miniseries follows the chess prodigy Beth Harmon?
questions.explanation: The Queen's Gambit, named after a chess opening, follows orphan Beth Harmon's rise to the top of the chess world.

questions.text: In Twin Peaks, whose murder sets off the investigation at the heart of the series?
questions.explanation: FBI agent Dale Cooper comes to Twin Peaks to investigate the killing of homecoming queen Laura Palmer.

questions.text: Which Muppet is the host of The Muppet Show?
questions.explanation: Jim Henson's Kermit the Frog hosts the show; Fozzie is a joke-telling bear, Gonzo a daredevil and Animal the wild drummer.

questions.text: Which Danish toy company is famous for its interlocking plastic bricks?
questions.explanation: LEGO comes from Billund, Denmark, and its name comes from the Danish leg godt, meaning play well. Playmobil is German.

questions.text: What is the name of Mario's brother?
questions.explanation: Luigi is Mario's brother. Wario is a different character, despite the similar name.

questions.text: Who is the princess of the Mushroom Kingdom?
questions.explanation: Peach is the Mushroom Kingdom's princess. Zelda belongs to The Legend of Zelda.

questions.text: Which Mario character is a green dinosaur?
questions.explanation: Yoshi is Mario's dinosaur companion. Bowser is the spiny-shelled antagonist, not Yoshi.

questions.text: Which hero is usually the playable protagonist of The Legend of Zelda?
questions.explanation: Link is usually the playable hero; Zelda is the princess whose name appears in the series title.

questions.text: Which yellow Pokemon is known for its electric powers and red cheeks?
questions.explanation: Pikachu's electric powers, yellow body and red cheeks distinguish it from the other Pokemon listed.

questions.text: Which original Kanto starter has a plant bulb on its back?
questions.explanation: Bulbasaur has a bulb on its back. Charmander has a flame-tipped tail, and Squirtle has a shell.

questions.text: What type is the original Pokemon Squirtle?
questions.explanation: Squirtle is a Water-type Pokemon. It is one of the original Kanto starter choices.

questions.text: Which blue video-game hedgehog is famous for speed?
questions.explanation: Sonic is the fast blue hedgehog. Kirby is a pink Nintendo character, not a hedgehog.

questions.text: Which company created the PlayStation brand?
questions.explanation: PlayStation is Sony's console brand; Nintendo and Sega have their own gaming histories.

questions.text: Which company created the Xbox brand?
questions.explanation: Xbox is Microsoft's console brand, while PlayStation belongs to Sony.

questions.text: In Minecraft, which green mob approaches players and explodes?
questions.explanation: Creepers explode near players. Endermen and villagers have different behaviors.

questions.text: Which Minecraft tool is designed for mining stone and ores?
questions.explanation: A pickaxe mines stone and ores. A hoe prepares farmland, while shears serve other gathering tasks.

questions.text: In Tetris, how many small squares form each standard falling piece?
questions.explanation: Standard Tetris pieces are tetrominoes: shapes made from four connected squares.

questions.text: What do players try to form to clear blocks in standard Tetris?
questions.explanation: Standard Tetris clears a row when it is filled horizontally, without gaps.

questions.text: In classic Pac-Man, what pursues Pac-Man around the maze?
questions.explanation: The classic maze enemies are ghosts; avoiding them is part of Pac-Man's core challenge.

questions.text: Which game series features the treasure hunter Lara Croft?
questions.explanation: Lara Croft is the Tomb Raider protagonist. Uncharted features a different treasure hunter.

questions.text: Which game series features the armored hero Master Chief?
questions.explanation: Master Chief is a central Halo hero. The other listed games feature different protagonists.

questions.text: In Among Us, which role secretly sabotages and eliminates crewmates?
questions.explanation: Impostors work against the crew while concealing their role; crewmates try to identify them.

questions.text: Which game combines car driving with soccer?
questions.explanation: Rocket League uses cars to hit a ball into goals. The other options are primarily racing games.

questions.text: Which Nintendo character is a pink hero who inhales enemies?
questions.explanation: Kirby is the pink character known for inhaling enemies; Yoshi and Toad have different abilities.

questions.text: In which country was Tetris created, in 1984?
questions.explanation: Alexey Pajitnov designed Tetris at a computer centre in Moscow; Nintendo's Game Boy version later turned it into a worldwide hit.

questions.text: Which 1972 Atari arcade game simulated table tennis?
questions.explanation: With two paddles and a bouncing ball, Pong became one of the first commercially successful video games.

questions.text: Which game designer created both Mario and The Legend of Zelda?
questions.explanation: Miyamoto created both series at Nintendo; Hideo Kojima is known for Metal Gear, and Yuji Naka co-created Sonic.

questions.text: In Pokemon games, what item do trainers throw to catch wild Pokemon?
questions.explanation: Poke Balls capture Pokemon; the Pokedex is an electronic encyclopedia that records the species a trainer encounters.

questions.text: What was Mario called in the original 1981 Donkey Kong arcade game?
questions.explanation: He was known as Jumpman and worked as a carpenter, not a plumber, before Nintendo named him Mario.

questions.text: In gaming, what does the abbreviation RPG stand for?
questions.explanation: In an RPG the player takes on a character's role and grows stronger over time, as in Final Fantasy or Pokemon.

questions.text: Which handheld console did Nintendo release in 1989?
questions.explanation: The Game Boy launched in 1989 and was famously bundled with Tetris; the Game Gear was Sega's rival handheld.

questions.text: In Minecraft, which dimension do players reach through an obsidian portal lit with fire?
questions.explanation: A lit obsidian frame opens a Nether portal; The End is reached through a different portal found in strongholds.

questions.text: Which 1978 Taito arcade game has players shooting rows of descending aliens?
questions.explanation: Tomohiro Nishikado's Space Invaders sparked an arcade boom; Namco's Galaga, with similar alien waves, came later in 1981.

questions.text: In Pokemon, which of these types is super effective against Water-type Pokemon?
questions.explanation: Grass attacks deal double damage to Water types, while Water is itself strong against Fire, Rock and Ground.

questions.text: Which fire-breathing Koopa king often kidnaps Princess Peach?
questions.explanation: Bowser rules the Koopas and is Mario's archenemy; Ganondorf is the main villain of The Legend of Zelda.

questions.text: In which fictional kingdom are most Legend of Zelda games set?
questions.explanation: Hyrule is Zelda's home kingdom; Tamriel belongs to The Elder Scrolls, Azeroth to Warcraft and Lordran to Dark Souls.

questions.text: What is the name of Sonic's two-tailed fox sidekick?
questions.explanation: Miles "Tails" Prower can fly by spinning his two tails; Knuckles is an echidna and Shadow is a hedgehog.

questions.text: Which studio originally developed Minecraft?
questions.explanation: Markus Persson created Minecraft and founded Mojang to develop it; Microsoft bought the studio in 2014. Bungie is known for Halo.

questions.text: Which Epic Games title popularized a battle royale mode where players build structures?
questions.explanation: Fortnite's free Battle Royale mode, launched in 2017, lets players build walls and ramps; PUBG is a battle royale without building.

questions.text: What is the name of the red ghost in classic Pac-Man?
questions.explanation: Blinky is red and chases Pac-Man most directly; Pinky is pink, Inky is cyan and Clyde is orange.

questions.text: What kind of animal is Donkey Kong?
questions.explanation: Donkey Kong is a gorilla who first appeared as the villain of the 1981 arcade game that also introduced Mario.

questions.text: Which game series stars the Spartan warrior Kratos?
questions.explanation: Kratos battles the gods of Greek and later Norse mythology in God of War; Devil May Cry stars the demon hunter Dante.

questions.text: Which fighting game series features the ninjas Scorpion and Sub-Zero?
questions.explanation: Scorpion and Sub-Zero are Mortal Kombat's rival ninjas; Street Fighter's best-known fighters are Ryu and Ken.

questions.text: Which was Sega's final home console before it left the hardware business in 2001?
questions.explanation: The Dreamcast launched in 1998; Sega stopped making consoles in 2001 and became a game publisher. The Saturn came just before it.

questions.text: What kind of toy is Woody in Toy Story?
questions.explanation: Woody is a cowboy doll, contrasting with Buzz Lightyear's space-ranger design.

questions.text: Which Toy Story character is a space ranger toy?
questions.explanation: Buzz Lightyear is the space ranger toy; Woody is the cowboy toy.

questions.text: Who owns Woody at the start of Toy Story (1995)?
questions.explanation: Andy owns Woody at the beginning of the original film. Bonnie becomes important later in the series.

questions.text: What is the name of Nemo's father in Finding Nemo?
questions.explanation: Marlin is Nemo's father and searches for him. Bruce is a shark, and Crush is a turtle.

questions.text: What kind of fish are Nemo and Marlin?
questions.explanation: Nemo and Marlin are clownfish, recognizable by their orange bodies and white bands.

questions.text: Which Finding Nemo character has short-term memory loss?
questions.explanation: Dory's difficulty forming short-term memories shapes her role in the search for Nemo.

questions.text: In Monsters, Inc., what do Sulley and Mike call the little human girl?
questions.explanation: Boo is the nickname Mike and Sulley use for the human child who enters their world.

questions.text: How many eyes does Mike Wazowski have?
questions.explanation: Mike Wazowski has one large eye, a central part of his character design.

questions.text: Inside Out (2015) takes place partly inside whose mind?
questions.explanation: Riley is the child whose emotions we follow; Joy and Sadness are emotions inside her mind.

questions.text: Which Inside Out emotion is represented by a blue character?
questions.explanation: Sadness is blue. Joy is mainly yellow, Anger is red, and Disgust is green.

questions.text: What animal is Remy in Ratatouille?
questions.explanation: Remy is a rat with a talent for cooking, not a mouse or hamster.

questions.text: In which city does Remy pursue cooking in Ratatouille?
questions.explanation: Ratatouille places Remy's cooking adventure in Paris, with a French restaurant at its center.

questions.text: What is the name of the young aspiring musician in Coco?
questions.explanation: Miguel is the young musician at the center of Coco. Hector and Ernesto are other characters.

questions.text: Coco centers on which Mexican holiday?
questions.explanation: Coco explores the Day of the Dead and remembrance of family; it is not about Cinco de Mayo.

questions.text: What lifts Carl's house into the sky in Up?
questions.explanation: Carl uses a large cluster of balloons to lift his house rather than an engine.

questions.text: What is the name of the talking dog in Up?
questions.explanation: Dug is the dog whose collar lets his thoughts be heard as speech.

questions.text: Which animated film features the race car Lightning McQueen?
questions.explanation: Lightning McQueen is the racing protagonist of Cars. Planes focuses on aircraft instead.

questions.text: What is WALL-E programmed to collect and compact on Earth?
questions.explanation: WALL-E compacts discarded trash into cubes as part of his cleanup task.

questions.text: What is the name of the Scottish princess in Brave?
questions.explanation: Merida is Brave's Scottish princess, known for her archery and independent spirit.

questions.text: Which Pixar family includes superheroes named Violet and Dash?
questions.explanation: The Parr family is the superhero family in The Incredibles; Violet and Dash are two of the children.

questions.text: What was Walt Disney's first full-length animated feature film?
answers: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
questions.explanation: Snow White (1937) was Disney's first animated feature; Pinocchio and Fantasia followed in 1940, and Bambi in 1942.

questions.text: In Frozen, what is the name of the snowman Elsa brings to life?
questions.explanation: Olaf is the friendly snowman created by Elsa's magic; Sven is Kristoff's reindeer and Hans is the scheming prince.

questions.text: In The Lion King (1994), who is Simba's father?
questions.explanation: Mufasa is king of the Pride Lands; Scar is his jealous brother, Simba's uncle, who plots his death.

questions.text: What kind of creature is Shrek?
questions.explanation: Shrek is a swamp-dwelling ogre; his 2001 film won the first-ever Oscar for Best Animated Feature.

questions.text: In Moana, which demigod joins Moana on her ocean voyage?
questions.explanation: Maui is a shape-shifting demigod from Polynesian legend; Tamatoa is a treasure-hoarding giant crab.

questions.text: Where does SpongeBob SquarePants live in Bikini Bottom?
questions.explanation: SpongeBob lives in a pineapple; Patrick lives under a rock and Squidward in a house shaped like an Easter Island head.

questions.text: Which animated TV family lives in the town of Springfield?
questions.explanation: Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa and Maggie Simpson live in Springfield; Family Guy's Griffins live in Quahog, Rhode Island.

questions.text: What is the name of the panda who becomes the Dragon Warrior in Kung Fu Panda?
questions.explanation: Po is the noodle-loving panda; Shifu, his teacher, is a red panda, and Master Oogway is a tortoise.

questions.text: In Disney's Aladdin (1992), what is the name of Aladdin's pet monkey?
questions.explanation: Abu is Aladdin's monkey sidekick; Iago is Jafar's parrot and Rajah is Princess Jasmine's tiger.

questions.text: Which Japanese studio made My Neighbor Totoro?
questions.explanation: Studio Ghibli was founded in 1985 by Hayao Miyazaki, Isao Takahata and Toshio Suzuki; Totoro even appears in its logo.

questions.text: Which Hayao Miyazaki film won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature at the 2003 ceremony?
